puranas.introduction:
The Puranas are a large body of Sanskrit literature that preserve sacred history, cosmology, devotional traditions, and ethical guidance. They present philosophy through narrative—stories of sages and kings, teachings on worship and duty, and reflections on time cycles and creation.

Traditionally, the Puranas are grouped into the Mahapuranas and Upapuranas, with many texts closely associated with particular deities and devotional lineages. As living tradition, the Puranas have shaped temple culture, festivals, pilgrimage, and household devotion across India for centuries.

scripture_text.content: Many Puranas are described as containing the classic five themes (panchalakshana): creation (sarga), recreation after dissolution (pratisarga), genealogies (vamsha), cosmic epochs and Manu cycles (manvantara), and dynastic histories (vamshanucharita). In practice, each Purana also includes hymns, dialogues, ethical teachings, pilgrimage guides, and sections on ritual and devotion.

Puranic stories are often multi-layered: they can be read as devotion (bhakti), as moral instruction (dharma), and as symbolic teaching about the mind, time, and the relationship between the individual self and the divine. This site treats them as a devotional-philosophical tradition, not merely as folklore.

puranas.philosophical_explanation:
The Puranas transmit philosophical ideas in an accessible form. Instead of presenting doctrine only through abstraction, they use characters, vows, crises, and transformations to show how dharma is applied under real-world pressure. Their cosmology teaches cyclical time and impermanence, while devotional sections cultivate surrender, gratitude, and inner steadiness.

For many readers, the Puranas serve as a bridge: from story and worship to deeper inquiry into the Upanishadic vision of the Self, the nature of reality, and liberation (moksha).
